vignette: Kai Chen, a 36-year-old tax consultant and married veteran of two tours in Afghanistan, sits stiffly in his office chair, avoiding eye contact. He has come to believe that any form of physical contact with others will set him off, like the time he was caught in an ambush during a patrol. The memories still linger vividly - the smell of smoke, the taste of sand, and the overwhelming chaos that followed. He can recall every detail when the memory returns, but it's the taste that lingers longest on his tongue. When someone touches him unexpectedly, Kai startles, reacting with alarm as if he's back in combat mode. This has made social interactions difficult; he avoids being touched at all costs and even flinches when his wife reaches out to hold his hand. "It feels like a threat, always lurking just beneath the surface," he explains, describing how unusual silence makes him feel something is about to go terribly wrong. He's developed a habit of identifying escape routes before he feels comfortable in any new space - a remnant of his military training that now serves as an anxiety-reducing strategy. Confrontations and confrontational conversations are also potent triggers for Kai, sending him spiraling back into the depths of the traumatic event. Talking with others about it only makes things worse, so he's learned to push away positive emotions because they feel "unsafe" - like letting his guard down will invite another attack. These maladaptive strategies have become ingrained over time; Kai avoids talking about the event or its aftermath, often changing the subject when his wife tries to discuss it. However, this avoidance behavior has an ironic side effect: the more he suppresses memories of the traumatic event, the more they seem to resurface in vivid detail. When the memory returns, Kai feels overwhelmed by emotion and has to stop whatever he's doing; at other times, he can recall what happened with eerie detachment, as if it had occurred to a stranger. This numbness is unsettling - like his emotions are "stuck," unable to process or release. Feeling physically unwell also sends Kai into a tailspin, reminding him of the long periods spent in dusty, cramped conditions during his tours. His mind begins racing with catastrophic scenarios, and he becomes convinced that something terrible will happen if he's not constantly vigilant. In response, Kai redoubles his escape route planning and avoidance behaviors - an attempt to regain control over his environment. Kai's relationships are suffering as a result; his wife feels like she's walking on eggshells around him, never knowing when he'll be triggered by some innocuous comment or gesture. At work, he finds himself increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with clients who seem oblivious to the fragility of life. What frightens Kai most is losing control - being "swept back" into the nightmare world of his memories and unable to escape. It's this fear that has finally brought him to seek help; Kai knows he needs to find a way out of this self-reinforcing cycle before it destroys everything he holds dear. For now, though, the memories linger - like an open wound refusing to heal.
